description: North German frontier march (1157–1618) created by Albert the Bear's conquest of Slavic territories; its position at the Elbe-Oder crossing made it the springboard for German eastward colonisation, while the Hohenzollern acquisition (1415) began the dynasty that would eventually create modern Germany, making Brandenburg a pivotal hinge in European history.

lifecycle_phases.description: Albert the Bear conquers Brandenburg from the Slavic Hevelli.
Ascanian expansion east and north; Brandenburg a major imperial electorate.
Dynastic transfers: Wittelsbach, Luxembourg; sold to Hohenzollern 1415.

rise_factors.description: German Ostsiedlung eastward colonization provided settlers, capital, and economic development of new territories.
Albert the Bear established the Ascanian military march with systematic castle-building and garrison organization.
Ascanian margraves systematically acquired adjacent Slavic territories through warfare and purchase.
The Hohenzollern dynasty acquired Brandenburg in 1415 and systematically built up centralized administration, integrating the scattered Ascanian inheritance into a coherent territorial state.

Brandenburg's position on the North German Plain gave it control over river crossings and roads linking the Rhine, Oder, and Vistula river systems, strategic importance that justified sustained imperial investment in its defense.

decline_factors.description: Ascanian line died out in 1320, leaving Brandenburg contested between Wittelsbach and Luxembourg dynasties.
Brandenburg was divided and sold among competing dynastic claims through the 14th century.
Repeated changes of ruling house undermined institutional continuity.

Brandenburg suffered extreme devastation during the Thirty Years War (1618–48), with half its population dying from war, plague, and famine, temporarily making it one of the most depopulated regions in Central Europe.

The margraviate was superseded by the Kingdom of Prussia in 1701 when Elector Frederick III crowned himself King in Prussia, elevating Brandenburg from a march to the nucleus of a major European power.
